description: We are a group of Data Science students from Chile looking to apply our knowledge into real life problems.
summary:
We have created an app that takes over five decades of annual precipitation in northern, central, and southern Chile, in order to detect, quantify, and communicate how the water falling over the country is changing.
Not only does our app collect this data, but it also allows the user to view the differences between areas through an interactive map of Chile, including information such as historical events regarding rain, annual precipitation, and questionnaires.
details:
This project develops an interactive analysis and visualization platform to study precipitation trends across three macro-zones in Chile (North, Center, and South). Its main source is NASA's GPM IMERG satellite product (1998–2025), complemented by a historical annual precipitation record (1970–2025). Both sources are analyzed independently to translate climate data into accessible metrics on rainfall variability, drought, and long-term change. Beyond the trend analysis, the platform includes a context section that places rainfall alongside known climate events, wildfires, and water legislation through an interactive timeline, a heatmap of dry and wet years across zones, and a before-and-after-2010 comparison, always stating explicitly that correlation does not imply causation. The site also offers a light and dark mode, and outlines future work linking precipitation to wildfires, urban expansion, environmental legislation, and other territorial factors.

The tools that we used to develop our website are:

  • Python 3 with Pandas: data cleaning and annual aggregation.
  • HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript: web interface and statistical calculations in the browser.
  • Plotly.js: interactive charts.
  • Visual Studio Code with the Live Server extension for local testing.
  • GitHub Pages: hosting of the public website.

Our website is a creative solution to this issue, because it allows the user to easily choose and view changes in Chile´s rain over time. Anyone—even without a background in statistics—can understand what is happening with rainfall in their area and how confident we can be in that information. For students, journalists, and decision-makers, this offers an honest way to interpret the data: we show what the data says, as well as what it cannot yet tell us.

Details on the AI tools that we used:

  • Gemini: Understanding how to navigate the site Giovanni.
  • Claude: Web development, processing data.
